rapc-01-c2.quote: After me there shall be no prophetess, but the end.
rapc-01-c2.claim: The fourth-century heresy-hunter Epiphanius quotes Maximilla as saying that after her there would be no more prophet, but the end.

rapc-03-c1.quote: He was born in Ottoman Izmir (Smyrna) in 1626
rapc-03-c1.claim: Sabbatai Zevi was born in 1626 in Smyrna (modern Izmir), a booming Ottoman port.

rapc-04-c1.quote: I am fully convinced that somewhere between March 21st, 1843, and March 21st, 1844, according to the Jewish mode of computation of time, Christ will come.
rapc-04-c1.claim: Pressed for precision, he said Christ would come sometime between 21 March 1843 and 21 March 1844, a Jewish year by his reckoning.

rapc-05-c3.quote: According to Jehovah's Witnesses' beliefs, Christ returned in 1914 and was enthroned as King of Kings and Lord of Lords but his kingdom remains invisible
rapc-05-c3.claim: Over time 1914 was reinterpreted as the year Christ was invisibly enthroned as king in heaven and the "last days" began, which remains Witness teaching.

rapc-06-c2.text: Joshua J. Mark (2012). The Maya Calendar and the End of the World: Why the one does not substantiate the other. World History Encyclopedia.
rapc-06-c2.quote: The Long Count calendar begins 11 August 3114 BCE
rapc-06-c2.claim: The Classic Maya Long Count tallied days from a mythical starting point that corresponds, in the most widely used correlation, to 11 August 3114 BCE.
